610.title: The water you drink, the fire you light
610.hook: have you seen the water you drink, the fire you kindle, who made them (56:68–72)
610.tomorrow: None touch it but the purified
610.howItsDone: Many Muslims say bismillah before drinking and alhamdulillah after, and follow the Prophet's practice of drinking in sips with pauses for breath; these verses of Al-Waqi'ah are recited as a reminder to be grateful for ordinary things.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the foremost, the first to good, brought near. Your line was first in good.

Turn on a tap and water comes out. Click a lighter and there's a flame. Both happen so often they don't feel like events. Nobody stands at the sink amazed. Surah Al-Waqi'ah, after its great pictures of the Day, turns to the kitchen. It asks four short questions about four ordinary things: the seed of life, the crop, the water, the fire. Each starts the same way: have you seen? Have you really looked?

Verse sixty-eight. Pickthall: "Have ye observed the water which ye drink?" Then the question behind it: is it you who bring it down from the rain cloud, or are We the ones who send it? And a sharp line: if God willed, he could make it bitter, salt; so why don't you give thanks? The same pattern comes a few verses earlier, with the seed from which a person is made, and with the crop: you plant, but who makes it grow? Then the fire. Have you seen the fire you strike? Was it you who made its tree grow, or did God? The Arabs of the time struck fire from green wood. Commentators name two desert trees, markh and 'afar, whose branches were rubbed together to make a flame. Surah Ya-Sin says it too: God made fire for you out of the green tree. Verse seventy-three gives fire two jobs: a reminder, and a comfort for travelers in the desert, who needed it to cook, to keep warm, to be seen at night. These aren't trick questions. Nobody listening thought they made the rain. The point is the habit of asking. Every glass of water arrives from somewhere: a cloud, a river, a pipe someone laid. A hadith turns drinking into a small, slow act. Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ would breathe three times while drinking, three sips rather than one gulp. Three pauses, enough to notice what's in your hand.
screen: `HAVE YOU SEEN THE WATER YOU DRINK?` · `IT COULD HAVE BEEN BITTER.` · `FIRE FROM THE GREEN TREE.` · `THREE BREATHS WHILE DRINKING.`

segments.voice: Pour a glass of water, or picture one, and if you can, light a candle safely and watch the flame for a few breaths. Then drink slowly, in three sips, letting today's question rise with each: who made it? If you pray, you can begin with bismillah and end with alhamdulillah.
Afara'aytum: have you seen? The question Surah Al-Waqi'ah asks four times, of the water, the seed, the crop and the fire. Today's word.
Your line: who made it? Every glass of water arrives from somewhere. That's day six hundred ten.

611.title: None touch it but the purified
611.hook: a noble Qur'an in a guarded book, touched only by the purified (56:77–79)
611.tomorrow: He is with you wherever you are
611.howItsDone: Most Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it in a high, clean place, and often wrap it in cloth; reciting from memory without wudu is widely permitted, and schools differ on details.

segments.voice: Yesterday: afara'aytum, have you seen, asked of the water and the fire. Your line was who made it?

Walk into many Muslim homes and you'll find the Qur'an on the highest shelf, often wrapped in cloth, nothing stacked on top. When someone takes it down, they may pause, go and wash, and come back. Children learn not to put it on the floor. A guest might be surprised by all the care around one book. Much of it traces back to three verses near the end of Surah Al-Waqi'ah, and what those verses mean, Muslim scholars have discussed, with more than one answer, for a very long time.

Verses seventy-seven to seventy-nine. Pickthall: "That (this) is indeed a noble Qur'an In a Book kept hidden Which none toucheth save the purified". Three things. The Qur'an is karim, noble, generous. It is in a kitab maknun, a book kept hidden, guarded. And none touches it but the mutahharun, the purified. Here the readings divide. Many classical commentators said the hidden book is the heavenly original, the preserved tablet, and the purified who touch it are the angels. On that reading, the verse describes the Qur'an's source, not a rule for people. Others read it as also pointing to the written copy on earth, the mushaf. And most jurists, whichever reading they held, required ritual purity to touch the mushaf. They leaned as well on a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to 'Amr ibn Hazm in Yemen, preserved in Malik's Muwatta: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure. So the four main Sunni schools, and Shia jurists too, generally hold that you should be in wudu, the washing before prayer, to touch the written Arabic text. A minority of scholars, among them Ibn Hazm of Andalusia, didn't require it. Reciting from memory without wudu is widely allowed. Whatever the ruling, the habit it built is the one in the hook: the book isn't just picked up. It's prepared for. The washing comes first, and the reading after.
screen: `A NOBLE QUR'AN, A BOOK KEPT HIDDEN.` · `THE PURIFIED: ANGELS, SAY MANY.` · `THE LETTER TO 'AMR IBN HAZM.` · `WASH FIRST, THEN READ.`

segments.voice: If you're Muslim, you might make wudu now, slowly, noticing the water on hands, mouth, face, arms, head and feet, then sit before you open the Qur'an. If that isn't yours, wash your hands and face slowly, with full attention, and come back to sit before whatever you read next. Let the water be the beginning of the reading.
Mutahharun: the purified, those alone said to touch the guarded book that holds a noble Qur'an, honored on earth with wudu. Today's word.

612.title: He is with you wherever you are
612.hook: He is with you wherever you are (57:4)
612.howItsDone: Some Muslims recall this verse when traveling or in unfamiliar places; the idea of ihsan, worshipping as though one sees God, is taught from the hadith of Jibril, where it follows islam and iman.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Al-Waqi'ah: mutahharun, the purified, and your line, touched with purity. Today, Surah Al-Hadid, the Iron.

An airport gate at 5am. A hospital corridor. A new apartment with the boxes still taped shut. A hotel room in a city where you don't speak the language. Places like these can make a person feel strangely unhooked, as if they've left their whole life at the last address. Surah fifty-seven, Al-Hadid, has a short line for exactly that feeling. It sits in the middle of a verse about the heavens and the Throne.

Al-Hadid opens wide: everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies God. Verse three gives four names in a row: he is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward. Verse four describes God creating the heavens and the earth in six days, then establishing himself on the Throne. He knows what goes into the earth and what comes out, what comes down from the sky and what goes up into it. And then, in Pickthall: "and He is with you wheresoever ye may be." Wa huwa ma'akum ayna ma kuntum. Ma'akum: with you. Ayna ma kuntum: wherever you are. The verse ends: and God sees what you do. So how is God with you? Muslims have explained it in more than one way. Commentators such as Ibn Kathir said he is with you by his knowledge, hearing and sight, watching over you, while being above his Throne, as the same verse says. Others, among them Sufi writers, dwell on the nearness itself, and read it with another verse: God is nearer to a person than their jugular vein. Both readings agree on one thing: in the verse, no place is out of his sight. The hadith of Jibril turns this into a way of worshipping. Asked what ihsan, excellence, is, the Prophet ﷺ said: to worship God as though you see him, and if you don't see him, he sees you. The airport gate, the hospital, the empty apartment: the verse doesn't make them less strange. It says you didn't arrive there alone.

613.title: Hearts not yet soft?
613.hook: has the time not come for believers' hearts to humble themselves (57:16)
613.howItsDone: Muslim preachers and teachers often recite 57:16 as a call to renewed sincerity, and the story of Fudayl ibn 'Iyad's turning is widely told in sermons and books on repentance.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ma'akum, God is with you, and your line, wherever you are.

There's a story told about a man named Fudayl ibn 'Iyad. In his youth, the story goes, he was a highway robber. One night he was climbing a wall to meet someone he shouldn't, and from a house nearby he heard a voice reciting the Qur'an. One verse, a question. He stopped on the wall and answered it out loud: yes, Lord, the time has come. He climbed down a different man, and the story remembers him afterward as an ascetic and a teacher.
screen: `A ROBBER ON A WALL AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Hadid, verse sixteen. Pickthall: "Is not the time ripe for the hearts of those who believe to submit to Allah's reminder and to the truth which is revealed". It opens: alam ya'ni lilladhina amanu an takhsha'a qulubuhum. Notice who's asked. Not unbelievers: those who believe, people who already pray and already know the words. Has the time not come for their hearts to soften? The verb is takhsha'a, from khushu', the humble stillness meant to fill prayer. A heart with khushu' has stopped resisting. Sahih Muslim preserves a striking line from the companion Ibn Mas'ud: between the time they accepted Islam and the time God reproached them with this verse, there were only four years. Four years in, and already the question: have you gotten used to it? The verse warns against hearts that grow hard as time stretches on. Then the next verse offers the turn: know that God brings the earth back to life after its death. A dead field after rain. Commentators read the two together: hardness isn't permanent, and a heart can be revived the way the ground is. Read that way, the Fudayl story, whatever its historical details, is the next verse acted out: a hard heart turned over in one night. And the question has no date written on it. It stays open, for whoever hears it.
screen: `ASKED OF THOSE WHO BELIEVE.` · `KHUSHU': A HEART THAT STOPS RESISTING.` · `ONLY FOUR YEARS IN.` · `THE EARTH REVIVED AFTER ITS DEATH.`

segments.voice: Notice where you hold tension, jaw, shoulders, hands, and let it soften. Then hold one place your heart has gone hard, a grudge, a habit you've stopped noticing, a person you've stopped listening to, without fixing it, and ask quietly: has the time not come? On each out-breath, let a little of it loosen.
Khushu': the humble stillness of a softened heart, which Surah Al-Hadid asks believers whether the time has come to have. Today's word.
Your line: has the time not come? Hard ground comes back after rain. That's day six hundred thirteen.

614.title: Play and amusement
614.hook: this life is play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth (57:20)
614.howItsDone: Muslim preachers often recite 57:20 in reminders about the passing nature of worldly life, while the hadith tradition also preserves room for play, sport and celebration, especially on the two Eids.

segments.voice: Yesterday: khushu', the softened heart, and your line, has the time not come?

A toddler with a plastic bucket on the beach. A teenager scrolling at midnight. A thirty-year-old choosing the right outfit for a wedding. A forty-year-old mentioning, casually, the new car. A seventy-year-old counting grandchildren and property. Five people wanting five different things. Surah Al-Hadid, verse twenty, lines up five words in a row, and some commentators have read them as exactly that: one life, from the beach to the end.

Pickthall: "Know that the life of the world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry, and boasting among you, and rivalry in respect of wealth and children". In Arabic, the five are la'ib, play; lahw, amusement or diversion; zina, adornment; tafakhur, boasting to one another; and takathur, piling up more wealth and children than the next person. Some commentators noticed the order follows the stages of a life: the child plays, the youth is diverted, the young adult adorns, the grown person boasts, the old person counts what they've gathered. Then a picture: rain brings up plants that delight the farmer. Then they dry, turn yellow, and become straw. Green, yellow, straw: the life of the world in one season. And in the next verse, a turn: race one another toward forgiveness from your Lord, and a garden as wide as the heavens and the earth. Is the verse against fun? The hadith collections suggest not. Bukhari records that the Prophet ﷺ let 'A'isha watch a group of Abyssinians performing with spears in the mosque on a feast day, standing so she could see over his shoulder until she'd had enough. The verse isn't banning the beach bucket. It's naming what play is: lovely, and passing, like grass after rain. Its warning is against mistaking it for the whole of life.
screen: `PLAY, AMUSEMENT, ADORNMENT.` · `BOASTING, AND PILING UP MORE.` · `GREEN, YELLOW, STRAW.` · `RACE TOWARD FORGIVENESS.`

615.title: Iron sent down
615.hook: We sent down iron with great strength and many uses (57:25)
615.howItsDone: Muslims read 57:25 as a summary of the messengers' mission: guidance, justice, and the strength to uphold it; the surah takes its name, Al-Hadid, from this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lahw, amusement, lovely and passing, and your line, play passes. Today, the verse that names Surah Al-Hadid.

Look around the room you're in. The nails in the walls. The hinges on the door. The frame of the chair, the spring in the pen, the steel inside the concrete. A kitchen knife, a hospital bed, a bridge, a sword. A great deal of modern life runs on iron, for building and for breaking. Surah fifty-seven is named Al-Hadid, the Iron, after one verse near its end, and that verse puts iron in surprising company: right beside scripture and the scales of justice.

Verse twenty-five, in paraphrase. God sent his messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Book and the Balance, so that people would stand up for justice. And God sent down iron, in which there is great strength and many benefits for people, and so that God may know who helps him and his messengers, unseen. Three things in one verse. The Book: guidance, what's right. The Balance: the mizan from Ar-Rahman, fairness, justice. And iron: power, the means to build, protect and defend. Commentators read them as a set. Guidance tells you what is just. The balance measures it. And iron is the strength that can protect justice or crush it. The striking part is the verb: anzalna, we sent down, the same verb used for the Qur'an itself. What does it mean to send down iron? Classical commentators pointed to Surah Az-Zumar, where God is said to have sent down cattle for people, eight kinds. There, sent down means created and provided as a gift from above. Some modern readers connect the verse to astronomy and the idea that iron came to the earth from beyond it. Others are cautious about reading science into a verse. Either way, the verse says something plain about strength: it's a trust. Iron has great power and many uses, and the same verse asks who will use it to help. The test isn't whether you have strength. It's which side of the balance you put it on.
screen: `THE BOOK, THE BALANCE, THE IRON.` · `STRENGTH TO PROTECT JUSTICE.` · `ANZALNA: WE SENT DOWN.` · `STRENGTH IS A TRUST.`

616.title: Allah heard her
616.hook: Allah heard the woman who argued with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, and a ruling came (58:1)
616.howItsDone: Muslims tell the story of Khawla bint Tha'laba as an example of a woman whose plea was answered in the Qur'an; Islamic law treats zihar as forbidden and sets an expiation before a husband who said it may return to his wife.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Al-Hadid: iron, strength sent down as a trust, and your line, strength sent down. Today, a surah named for a woman.

In a small room in Medina, a woman is speaking with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, low and urgent. Her husband, in anger, has said an old Arabian phrase to her: you are to me like my mother's back. By custom, that left a wife in limbo: not divorced, so she couldn't remarry, and not a wife, so he wouldn't come near her. She has children, and she's getting older. She argues her case. In a corner of the same house, the Prophet's wife 'A'isha can't even make out the words.

The reports name her Khawla bint Tha'laba, and her husband Aws ibn as-Samit. She pleaded, and she complained to God. And the surah that came down opens with her. Pickthall: "Allah hath heard the saying of her that disputeth with thee (Muhammad) concerning her husband, and complaineth unto Allah." Qad sami'a Allah: God has heard. The surah is named for her: Al-Mujadila, she who disputes, she who pleads her case. A whole surah, named for a woman who argued. The next verses settle the matter. Saying that phrase doesn't make a wife into a mother; it's a wrong and false thing to say. A man who says it and wants to return must make amends first: free a slave, or if he can't, fast two months in a row, or if he can't, feed sixty poor people. The custom that trapped women was ended. And 'A'isha's reaction is the part people remember. The reports preserve her words: blessed is the One whose hearing takes in every voice. The woman was speaking to the Prophet in a corner of my house, and I couldn't hear what she said, and God heard her from above the seven heavens. Notice what the verse doesn't do. It doesn't scold her for arguing. It records her disputing and her complaint, and answers both. A voice too low for the next room was heard, and the answer became law for everyone after her.
screen: `KHAWLA PLEADS HER CASE.` · `QAD SAMI'A ALLAH: GOD HAS HEARD.` · `AN OLD CUSTOM ENDED.` · `HEARING THAT TAKES IN EVERY VOICE.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you've been quietly unhappy about but haven't said, at home, at work, with a friend, and picture Khawla, low-voiced and steady. Shape what you need into one calm, clear sentence, no blame, just the truth of it; if you pray, bring it to God first, as she did.
Al-Mujadila: she who disputes, the surah named for Khawla, whose complaint to the Prophet, God says, he heard. Today's word.
Your line: she was heard. The week ran from the water you drink and the purified, through Al-Hadid's nearness, soft hearts, play and iron, to Khawla's quiet voice. Day six hundred sixteen.
